common_name: Madame Lemoine Lilac (Double White French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Madame Lemoine, introduced by Victor Lemoine in 1890 and named for his wife, remains one of the most widely planted double white lilacs.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air circulation, and deadhead the spent flower trusses promptly after bloom since next year's buds form soon afterward. Madame Lemoine produces densely packed double florets that open creamy and mature to a clean, pure white, carrying the classic heavy lilac fragrance on an upright, vigorous shrub. As with other common-lilac cultivars, thin out a few of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level every few years to keep flowering concentrated on younger wood rather than letting the shrub become a leggy thicket. It needs a real winter chill to set buds well and performs best where winters are cold enough to satisfy its dormancy requirement.

common_name: Charles Joly Lilac (Double Wine-Red French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Charles Joly, bred by Victor Lemoine in 1896, is among the darkest-colored of the classic French hybrid lilacs.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and remove faded flower clusters right after bloom before next year's buds set. Charles Joly bears fat, tightly double florets in a deep wine-red to magenta-purple that reads almost black in bud, making it one of the darkest-flowered lilacs commonly grown, and its fragrance is as strong as the species. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes to the base every few years to keep the shrub from becoming congested and to encourage strong new flowering wood. Like other common lilacs it needs a cold winter dormancy period and struggles to bloom well in mild-winter climates.

common_name: Katherine Havemeyer Lilac (Double Lavender-Purple French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; this Lemoine introduction, released in 1922, is prized as one of the most intensely fragrant double lilacs.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air movement, and deadhead spent trusses immediately after flowering since bud set for the following year begins soon after bloom. Katherine Havemeyer opens from purple-lavender buds into large, very double, richly fragrant florets that fade toward a soft pale lilac-pink as they age, giving the truss a two-toned look while in full flower. Thin a few of the oldest stems at ground level periodically to keep the shrub renewing itself and blooming on vigorous younger wood rather than becoming woody and sparse at the base. A sustained cold winter is needed to satisfy its chilling requirement and produce a full bloom the following spring.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Sensation, a 1938 Dutch introduction, is the best-known bicolor common lilac.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead faded clusters promptly after bloom. Sensation is grown for its unusual single florets of deep purple-red edged with a crisp, irregular white picotee margin, a striking pattern unlike any other common lilac cultivar. Because the bicolor pattern is genetically unstable, occasional branches will revert to solid purple flowers, and these reverted stems should be pruned out at their point of origin as soon as they are noticed to keep the plant true to type. Otherwise it is grown and maintained exactly like other Syringa vulgaris cultivars, needing a cold winter dormancy period and periodic renewal pruning of old canes.

common_name: Belle de Nancy Lilac (Double Rose-Pink French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Belle de Nancy, released by Victor Lemoine in 1891 and named for his home city of Nancy, France, is a classic double pink lilac.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air movement, and remove spent flower clusters right after bloom before next year's buds form. Belle de Nancy opens from carmine-pink buds into large, fully double florets that soften to a delicate rose-pink with lilac overtones as the truss matures, giving each cluster a shaded, multi-toned appearance. Periodically cut a few of the thickest, oldest canes back to the ground to stimulate fresh basal growth and keep flowering abundant rather than confined to the top of an increasingly woody shrub. It requires a cold winter to bloom reliably and, like other French hybrid lilacs, resents poorly drained or consistently wet soil.

common_name: President Lincoln Lilac (Single Blue French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; introduced by John Dunbar of the Rochester, New York parks system in 1916, President Lincoln was one of the first lilacs marketed as having true blue flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air circulation, and deadhead spent trusses soon after flowering finishes. President Lincoln carries single florets in a cool, soft blue-lavender that appears bluer than most common lilac cultivars, especially in the cooler light of early morning or on overcast spring days, and its fragrance is typical of the species. Maintain vigor with periodic removal of a few of the oldest canes at the base so new flowering wood keeps developing throughout the shrub. It needs a genuine cold winter dormancy period to flower well and, like other common lilacs, should not be planted in soil that stays wet.

common_name: Ludwig Spaeth Lilac (Single Deep Wine-Purple French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; introduced by the Spath nursery of Germany in 1883 under the name Andenken an Ludwig Spath, this remains one of the longest-cultivated dark-purple lilacs still sold today.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and remove faded flower clusters promptly after bloom since bud formation for next spring begins shortly afterward. Ludwig Spaeth produces single florets in a deep, saturated wine-purple, one of the darkest and most reliable colors among single-flowered common lilacs, held on an upright, vigorous, long-lived shrub. Thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level every few years to renew flowering wood and prevent the base from becoming bare and woody. It requires a cold winter dormancy period to bloom well and, once established, tolerates poor soil better than many newer cultivars as long as drainage is good.

common_name: Primrose Lilac (Single Pale Yellow French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Primrose, discovered as a branch sport by Dutch nurseryman D. Maarse in 1949, is the only widely grown common lilac cultivar with yellow flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air movement, and deadhead spent flower clusters soon after bloom. Primrose opens pale greenish-yellow buds into single florets of a soft, creamy primrose yellow, a color unique among common lilac cultivars, though the yellow tends to bleach toward cream in strong sun and fades further as each floret ages. Give it the same care as other common lilacs, including periodic renewal pruning of a few old canes at the base to keep flowering vigorous on younger wood. It needs a cold winter dormancy period to flower well and performs best in climates with a distinct chilling season.

common_name: Beauty of Moscow Lilac (Double Pearl-Pink-Budded White French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; bred by Leonid Kolesnikov in Russia and introduced in 1943 as Krasavitsa Moskvy, this cultivar is widely regarded as one of the finest lilacs ever raised.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and remove faded trusses right after flowering since next year's buds set soon after. Beauty of Moscow opens from soft pink buds into fully double, pearl-white florets that retain a faint pink blush at the base, creating a shimmering, two-toned effect across the truss that is one of the most photographed traits of any lilac cultivar. Renewal-prune a few of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep flowering concentrated on vigorous younger wood rather than an increasingly woody framework. Like other Syringa vulgaris selections it needs a real winter chill to flower well and should be planted in well-drained soil.

common_name: Yankee Doodle Lilac (Single Dark Purple Early French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Yankee Doodle was bred by lilac hybridizer Father John Fiala and introduced in the 1970s for its unusually dark, early-opening flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent flower clusters promptly after bloom. Yankee Doodle opens nearly black-purple buds into single florets of an intensely saturated dark purple, among the darkest colors found in common lilac cultivars, on a relatively compact, upright shrub that blooms a little earlier than many older French hybrids. Thin a few of the oldest canes at the base periodically to keep the plant renewing itself and flowering densely rather than becoming sparse and woody. It requires a cold winter dormancy period to bud well and, once established, is easy-care like other Syringa vulgaris selections.

common_name: Marechal Foch Lilac (Single Magenta-Pink French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; introduced by the Lemoine nursery in 1924 and named for French Marshal Ferdinand Foch, this cultivar is grown for its vivid magenta-pink flower color.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil with good air movement, and remove faded flower trusses soon after bloom before next year's buds set. Marechal Foch bears single florets in a vivid carmine-rose to magenta-pink, a bolder, warmer color than most common lilac cultivars, held in generously sized clusters with the typical strong lilac fragrance. Keep the shrub renewing itself by cutting a few of the oldest, thickest canes to the ground every few years rather than letting it become congested and top-heavy. It needs a cold winter dormancy period to flower well and, like other French hybrid lilacs, performs poorly in soil that stays wet.

common_name: Vestale Lilac (Single Pure White French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Vestale, introduced by Victor Lemoine in 1910, is regarded by lilac specialists as one of the finest single white common lilac cultivars ever raised.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent trusses right after flowering since bud set for the next season begins soon after. Vestale carries single florets of a clean, pure white in large, exceptionally full trusses, and it is noted among white lilac cultivars for unusually heavy, reliable flowering once established. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the shrub vigorous and flowering on younger wood rather than becoming leggy. It needs a genuine cold winter to set buds well and, like other common lilacs, should be sited in well-drained soil with good air circulation to limit powdery mildew.
